newsitem.title: UK: London doctor finds gentler way to fight cancer.
newsitem.headline: London doctor finds gentler way to fight cancer.

text.p: Researchers working in London said on Tuesday they may have found a way to make more widely available an immune system treatment touted as a more natural way to fight cancer.

They said they could mass-produce killer T-cells, which have been pre-programmed to seek out and destroy cancer cells. The procedure has only been tested in mice, but if it worked in people, it could offer a gentler alternative to chemotherapy.
Killer T-cells are immune system cells that eliminate invaders like bacteria and viruses, or defective cells such as cancer cells.

Hans Stauss and colleagues of the Royal Postgraduate Medical School at London's Hammersmith Hospital said a single healthy person may be able to produce enough such cells to help dozens of cancer patients.

Stauss, who presented his findings to a joint meeting of the British Society for Immunology and the Biochemical Society, said his research centred on a protein known as mdm-2 that is often produced in large amounts by cancer cells.

Scientists have already been able to separate T-cells from the blood of cancer patients as well as choose those that will attack the the tumour, grow them in a laboratory and re-inject them into the patient to fight the cancer.

But the procedure must be carried out for each individual patient, which is time-consuming and expensive. T-cells from one person will attack all kinds of cells in a stranger's body, not just cancer cells.

Stauss looked for a way to make the process a little less personal, and found if the T-cells could be programmed against one specific protein seen only in cancer cells, they would not be a danger to healthy cells.
The idea worked in mice, he told delegates at the meeting. "The (T-cells) were injected into mice with tumours and showed anti-cancer activity," conference organisers said in a statement.

"Dr Stauss' studies suggest that it may be possible to produce cancer fighting CTL to treat a large number of cancer patients from the blood of a single, healthy person, promising to make this gentle form of treatment easier and cheaper."
